summary: This informational memo discusses policies that require labels like Adv: in the Subject of messages. It argues they are hard to specify accurately while following key RFCs and are likely ineffective at best, and it describes a standards-compliant alternative.

plainLanguage.summary: Rules that force sellers to write 'Adv:' in the subject line do not work well. This document explains why and suggests a better way.

subtitle: Why policy-mandated labels like Adv: in email subject lines don't work and what to do instead.

tldr.problem: Many governments and organizations have laws requiring labels like 'Adv:' to be inserted in email subject lines to identify commercial messages, but the technical and practical challenges make these requirements nearly impossible to implement without loopholes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents why subject lines are a poor place for machine-readable labels—they are edited by software, have display limits on phones, conflict with other requirements, and can be worked around using encoding tricks.
tldr.outcome: The RFC recommends using a designated email header field like 'No-Solicit:' for machine-readable labels instead of overloading the subject line with mandatory markers.

today: RFC 4096 is an Informational RFC presenting a critical analysis of labeling requirements. It remains relevant to discussions of email filtering and anti-spam policy, though it is not obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Problem with Subject Line Labels
sections.content:
The U.S. CAN-SPAM Act of 2003 asked the Federal Trade Commission to consider whether commercial email messages should be identifiable by special labels like 'ADV:' in the subject line. Similar requirements have been enacted in Korea, Colorado, Florida, and many other jurisdictions. This RFC examines why this approach causes serious practical and technical problems.

The author, Carl Malamud, illustrates the difficulties through a hypothetical story: if every country and state applies its own labeling requirement, a single message might need to bear 'ADV:' (U.S.), '@' (Korea), 'legal advertisement' (Florida), and labels from dozens of other places, all crammed into a subject line. Different requirements for different message types create even more complexity.
sections.plainLanguage: Different countries and states want different labels on email ads, but trying to fit them all into the subject line creates a mess that spammers can easily get around.

sections.title: Why Subject Lines Are the Wrong Place
sections.content:
The RFC explains seven reasons why subject line labels fail. First, the subject line is not strictly limited and can be folded onto multiple lines, so labels get hidden. Second, phones and PDAs show only the first few dozen characters, so labels near the end are invisible. Third, many agents—mailing list software, filters, and email clients—add their own text to the subject line, making it cluttered and unreliable. Fourth, conflicting requirements from different jurisdictions cannot all be satisfied.

Most critically, the subject line serves humans, not machines. It is meant to convey the topic of a message in plain language, and injecting machine-readable tokens disrupts that purpose. A sender can use encoding tricks (like Hebrew character sets) to hide, obfuscate, or move labels, making them undetectable to the machines trying to filter on them. Drafting loophole-free regulations is nearly impossible.
sections.plainLanguage: Subject lines are too short, they get edited by email software, and clever senders can hide the labels using tricks like unusual character sets or very long subjects.

sections.title: An Alternative: Solicitation Class Keywords
sections.content:
RFC 3865 defined the solicitation class keyword, which allows labels to be placed in a dedicated email header field like 'No-Solicit:' instead of the subject line. These keywords are formatted like reversed domain names (e.g., 'com.example.adv' for a company's commercial messages). The mechanism is precise, simple to specify, and cannot be hidden or obfuscated.

This approach has advantages: it does not interfere with the subject line, it is easy for mail software to filter on reliably, senders can add multiple keywords (including ones that signal legitimate prior relationships), and mail transfer agents can insert keywords of their own. A policy maker can specify exactly what keyword format to use, and both senders and receivers can understand the rule without ambiguity.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of putting labels in the subject, use a special email header field designed just for labels. It is cleaner, easier to read and filter, and much harder to get around.

sections.title: Why Labels Create a False Sense of Security
sections.content:
Subject line labeling gives policy makers and users an illusion that messages are being automatically sorted and filtered correctly. In reality, the labels are easily hidden or defeated. This creates a false sense of protection. If people trust that 'Adv:' labels mean a message is truly commercial, they might relax their guard against cleverly disguised spam. Worse, if labels appear inconsistently or incorrectly, users may get tired of seeing them and start ignoring them altogether.

The RFC recommends avoiding subject line labeling entirely if possible, and if labeling is required by law, pairing it with a header-based alternative like 'No-Solicit:' so that mail software can filter reliably on a field that cannot be hidden.
sections.plainLanguage: People think subject line labels protect them from spam, but they do not—spammers just hide or fake the labels. A special header field would be much more trustworthy.
